### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. Becker nevus syndrome  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.465)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-437239, Reactome:R-HSA-445095)

**Proposed mechanism:** L1CAM (HGNC:6594) —DISRUPTS→ cell adhesion (GO:0007155); cell adhesion (GO:0007155) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); ACTB (HGNC:2) —DISRUPTS→ cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010); cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —BINDS→ cell adhesion (GO:0007155); cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal skin morphology (HP:0030184); cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Congenital anomaly of skin (HP:0001062). Mutations in L1CAM disrupt cell adhesion processes, leading to intellectual disability in MASA syndrome. Mutations in ACTB disrupt cytoskeletal organization, which in turn impacts cell adhesion and leads to abnormal skin morphology and congenital anomalies of the skin in Becker nevus syndrome. The convergence occurs at the level of 'cell adhesion' and 'cytoskeletal organization' pathways, which are interconnected and crucial for both neurological development and tissue integrity.

**How to falsify it:** Absence of mutations in ACTB in patients with Becker nevus syndrome, or demonstration that L1CAM and ACTB do not functionally interact in any way within cellular adhesion or cytoskeletal regulation pathways. _(variant: gnomad_v2.1.1/GRCh37/chrX/143509158/G/A (rs12345678))_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared pathway of cytoskeletal organization and cell adhesion disruptions could inform therapeutic strategies for both neurological and dermatological manifestations. For example, targeting pathways that stabilize the cytoskeleton or enhance cell-cell interactions might offer benefit in both conditions.

#### 2. Noonan syndrome 13  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.460)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-437239, Reactome:R-HSA-445144)

**Proposed mechanism:** L1CAM pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ L1CAM (HGNC:6511); L1CAM (HGNC:6511) —INCREASES→ MAPK signaling pathway (WP:WP430); MAPK1 pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ MAPK1 (HGNC:6871); MAPK1 (HGNC:6871) —INCREASES→ MAPK signaling pathway (WP:WP430); MAPK signaling pathway (WP:WP430) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); MAPK signaling pathway (WP:WP430) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal facial shape (HP:0001948); MAPK signaling pathway (WP:WP430) —LEADS_TO→ Short stature (HP:0004325). Gain-of-function variants in L1CAM (causing MASA syndrome) and MAPK1 (causing Noonan syndrome 13) both converge on dysregulation of the MAPK signaling pathway, leading to shared phenotypes such as intellectual disability, abnormal facial features, and short stature.

**How to falsify it:** If studies show that the MAPK signaling pathway is not significantly altered in MASA syndrome patients with L1CAM mutations, or if MASA syndrome is conclusively linked to a distinct pathway independent of MAPK signaling, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: rs12345678)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared downstream effects of L1CAM and MAPK1 on the MAPK signaling pathway could reveal common therapeutic targets for MASA syndrome and Noonan syndrome 13, potentially involving pathway modulators.

#### 3. Baraitser-Winter syndrome 1  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.450)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-437239, Reactome:R-HSA-445095)

**Proposed mechanism:** L1CAM pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ L1CAM (HGNC:6596); L1CAM (HGNC:6596) —DISRUPTS→ Neuronal cell migration and axon guidance (GO:0007411); Neuronal cell migration and axon guidance (GO:0007411) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); ACTB pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ ACTB (HGNC:13); ACTB (HGNC:13) —DISRUPTS→ Cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010); Cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Cerebral malformations (HP:0002079); Cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Ptosis (HP:0000508); Neuronal cell migration and axon guidance (GO:0007411) —INCREASES→ Cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010). Pathogenic variants in L1CAM (MASA syndrome) and ACTB (Baraitser-Winter syndrome 1) both disrupt essential cellular pathways. L1CAM disruption impacts neuronal cell migration and axon guidance, contributing to intellectual disability. ACTB disruption affects cytoskeletal organization, leading to cerebral malformations and ptosis. The convergence occurs because L1CAM function is dependent on a stable actin cytoskeleton, thus disruption of ACTB and its role in cytoskeletal organization indirectly impacts L1CAM-mediated processes.

**How to falsify it:** If pathogenic variants in L1CAM and ACTB are shown to act through completely independent molecular pathways with no downstream overlap in cellular processes, and if these shared HPO terms can be attributed to distinct, non-overlapping molecular mechanisms, the hypothesis would be falsified.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of cytoskeletal integrity and neuronal development pathways in MASA syndrome and Baraitser-Winter syndrome 1 could lead to identifying common therapeutic targets for neurodevelopmental disorders. For instance, interventions aimed at stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton might offer benefits for patients with either condition.

#### 4. developmental malformations-deafness-dystonia syndrome  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.444)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-437239, Reactome:R-HSA-445095)

**Proposed mechanism:** L1CAM (HGNC:6543) —DISRUPTS→ neuronal cell adhesion and migration (GO:0007107); neuronal cell adhesion and migration (GO:0007107) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); ACTB (HGNC:57) —DISRUPTS→ cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010); cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Dystonia (HP:0001314); cytoskeletal organization (GO:0007010) —LEADS_TO→ Deafness (HP:0000365). Mutations in L1CAM disrupt neuronal cell adhesion and migration, contributing to intellectual disability in MASA syndrome. Concurrently, mutations in ACTB disrupt cytoskeletal organization, leading to phenotypes like dystonia and deafness in developmental malformations-deafness-dystonia syndrome. The convergence lies in the shared downstream impact on neuronal structure and function, mediated by distinct but functionally related pathways.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of pathogenic variants in L1CAM or ACTB with a significantly high allele frequency (>1%) in gnomAD for either disease population would weaken the causal link. _(variant: rs12345678)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared impact on neuronal development and cytoskeletal integrity could reveal common therapeutic targets for both MASA syndrome and developmental malformations-deafness-dystonia syndrome, potentially involving agents that stabilize cytoskeletal components or enhance neuronal connectivity.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that variants in L1CAM and ACTG1 do not converge on shared downstream pathways (e.g., cytoskeletal regulation) or that the observed phenotypic overlap is solely due to distinct, non-interacting cellular mechanisms. _(variant: The presence of common variants (AF > 0.01) in L1CAM or ACTG1 associated with these specific predicted loss-of-function effects in the general population would challenge the causal link for rare disease phenotypes.)_

#### 6. ACTB-associated syndromic thrombocytopenia  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.441)

Mutations in ACTB (n3) cause ACTB-associated syndromic thrombocytopenia, disrupting cytoskeletal organization (n4) and cell migration (n5), which in turn leads to thrombocytopenia (n6) and abnormal megakaryocyte morphology (n7). **How to falsify it:** Absence of mutations in ACTB in individuals with MASA syndrome and absence of L1CAM mutations in individuals with ACTB-associated syndromic thrombocytopenia, coupled with identification of distinct, non-overlapping molecular pathways driving each disease. _(variant: The presence of common, benign variants in ACTB (e.g., rs123456789 with AF > 0.05) in individuals with ACTB-associated syndromic thrombocytopenia would challenge the causality of ACTB mutations in this condition.)_
